meaning: He who causes to be fertile (Egyptian sbk)

pronunciation.ipaLabel: Conventional reading — Egyptian vocalisation not attested

phonemes.desc: Written sbk; the s is a sibilant, the b a voiced bilabial stop.
Final k is consonantal. Egyptologists conventionally vocalise “Sobek”.

pronunciation.approximation: “SOH-bek” — already essentially the form used today
pronunciation.note: The name is related to sbk, “he who unites/causes to be pregnant” — a fertility sense built into the word.

domains.title: God of the Nile, Fertility, and Military Power
domains.subtitle: The Crocodile Who Rises from the River
domains.lead: Sbk — Sobek — is the crocodile god of the Nile’s dangerous fertility: the animal that kills at the water’s edge and the power that makes the flood bring life. In the Middle Kingdom he rose from local river god to a creator deity in his own right, and his cult centres — Crocodilopolis and Kom Ombo — kept living sacred crocodiles as his incarnations.

cards.name: Lord of the Waters
cards.desc: Master of the Nile and its inundation; the flood itself was called “the arrival of Sobek”.

cards.name: The Crocodile God
cards.desc: Incarnate in Crocodylus niloticus; temple pools held living sacred crocodiles adorned with jewellery.

cards.name: Creator and Solar Eye
cards.desc: In Middle Kingdom theology he emerges from the primordial waters; at Kom Ombo he shares a temple with Horus.

cards.name: Patron of the Army
cards.desc: Soldiers and the Pharaoh’s power; his epithets link him to strength and military might.

mythology.lead: Sobek has no single continuous myth-cycle; his theology was assembled from the river itself — the annual flood that could drown or feed — and from the pharaonic appetite for a god who united raw natural violence with legitimate kingship. The Middle Kingdom elevated him to cosmic rank: a creator who rises from the Nun, the primordial water.

myths.title: The Crocodile Who Emerges from Nun
myths.text: The Sobek theology of the Fayum — best preserved in the hymn cycles of the crocodile temples — casts him as the one who first climbed from the primeval waters, creator of the world’s order and of the Nile itself. Later tradition even made him a form of the sun god’s power, the fierce Eye of Ra returned from the Nubian desert.

myths.title: The Double Temple
myths.text: At Kom Ombo south of Luxor, Sobek shares a perfectly symmetrical double temple with Horus the Elder: one half for the falcon of the sky, one for the crocodile of the river. The division stages the Egyptian ideal of the Two Lands’ balance — sky and water, kingship and fertility — under one roof.

myths.title: Sobek and the Wonders at Court
myths.text: In the Westcar Papyrus’ cycle of Khufu-era wonders, the crocodile motif appears in the tale of the adulterer punished by a wax crocodile that comes alive at a word — a demonstration that the river-god’s animal is an instrument of moral order, released and recalled by priestly power.

myths.title: Petsuchos, the Sacred Crocodile
myths.text: Strabo and Herodotus describe the living god of Crocodilopolis: a great crocodile called Petsuchos, kept in a pool, fed by priests, adorned with gold and crystal rings. When it died the city mourned; a new Petsuchos was sought among the river animals by oracular selection — the god re-incarnating indefinitely.

lore.syncretism: Sobek absorbed and was absorbed: as Sobek-Ra he took solar status, while earlier he had fused with Horus as Sobek-Horus, lord of the Fayunite unity of king and river. The Greeks called his city Crocodilopolis and identified him with their own river-figures rather than a single Olympian; Roman-period Fayum mummy portraits from his cities remain among Egyptology’s most familiar images.
lore.culturalLegacy: The name Sobek survives in the modern scholarly vocabulary of the Nile and appears throughout Egyptological literature as the archetype of Egyptian theriolatry — the worship of a dangerous animal not despite but because of its power. The Fayum’s temple of Medinet Madi preserves the longest surviving sacred hymn cycles addressed to a crocodile.
lore.extendedMeditation: To restore Sbk is to keep the consonants the Egyptians trusted to carry a name across millennia of silence. The crocodile god needs no decoration: the word itself snaps shut like the animal — four letters, one vowel of uncertainty, the whole Nile behind it.

sources.name: Sobek hymns of Medinet Madi (Fayum temple liturgy)

lore.archaeology: Crocodilopolis (Shedet, modern Medinet el-Fayum) held the main temple; Kom Ombo’s double temple survives in superb relief, its columns carrying intact crocodile capitals. Crocodile cemeteries at Tebtunis and el-Shams el-Qawassim held mummified sacred crocodiles by the hundreds, each an embodied Sobek buried with honours.
lore.cult: His priests kept living crocodiles as cult statues made flesh; the animals were fed, adorned, and oracularly consulted, and at death mummified and buried in necropolises of their own. The Fayum’s Krokodilophoria festival carried the god’s image on procession; the flood season itself was his epiphany.
lore.iconography: Human-bodied with the head of a Crocodylus niloticus, crowned with ram’s horns, sun disc and uraeus when solar, or with the plumes and horns of Amun when fused as Sobek-Amun. His sacred colour is the green-blue of the inundation; the was-sceptre of power is his frequent attribute.
lore.reception: Greek and Roman travellers were fascinated and repelled in equal measure — Herodotus’ crocodile chapter opens with the tame-temple beast and closes with the mummification of the species. Sobek remains the standard example in comparative religion of the worship of dangerous fauna as a strategy of propitiation.
